stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1, the atonal mission
stops.campa: Five doors from Lenin's lodging, Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire draws Laban's dancers into its orbit: Sophie Taeuber, Käthe Wulff and Perrottet among the masks by Janco and the noise-poems read at the counter. Perrottet's own weapon is the piano: she gives the Dadaists the one thing none of them can supply for themselves, contemporary concert music, playing whole soirées of Schoenberg and Satie to ears that find it merely grotesque. The atlas's only Dada door opens here: abstract dance and atonal sound trading a single stage on the Spiegelgasse.
stops.quote: Das war meine Rolle bei den Dadaisten, die ganz moderne, neuzeitliche Musik dem Publikum vorführen. So spielte ich an etlichen Dada-Soiréen ausschliesslich Werke im atonalen Stil. Dem damaligen Publikum war diese Musik völlig unbekannt und kam ihnen für ihre Ohren grässlich vor.
stops.quote_source: Suzanne Perrottet, Ein bewegtes Leben, cited in 'Wie klang Dada?', Republik, 17 February 2022

stops.name: Kaufleuten, Zurich, the soirées continue
stops.campa: As the war drags on and the Dada evenings outgrow the Spiegelgasse cellar, they move to larger halls like the Kaufleuten, and Perrottet's atonal programs move with them, still the resident modernist among the noise-poets and mask-dancers. She is, by now, the connective tissue between two entirely separate revolutions happening in the same small city: the abolition of music in dance on one side of town, the abolition of sense in poetry on the other, and her own two hands at the keyboard translating Schoenberg into the gap between them.

stops.name: Monte Verità, Sang an die Sonne, the sun sung down and up
stops.campa: At the close of the great wartime congress on the mountain, Laban stages Sang an die Sonne across a whole night: the sun's descent danced at evening over the lake, the demons of midnight before Gräser's grotto, at dawn a choir greeting the sun as promise that the war will end. Perrottet dances among the torches, no longer the arriving collaborator of 1913 but a co-founder of the whole language being performed, priestess of a religion of the body she helped compose, while the guns still hold Europe beyond the lake.

stops.name: Zurich, Laban leaves, and the school becomes hers
stops.campa: At the end of the war Laban leaves Switzerland for Germany, where a shattered nation is hungry for exactly the choreographed mass-movement he can supply. He leaves behind the Zurich school, then housed in rooms borrowed from the Kunsthaus, and the woman who has kept its accounts, taught its classes and borne its founder's son. Perrottet takes over outright. What began as Dalcroze's Bildungsanstalt and became Laban's laboratory now becomes, without ceremony, simply hers: six decades of teaching about to begin under a single continuous roof.

stops.name: Zurich, the Schule für Eurythmie, renamed against confusion
stops.campa: She continues the school first jointly with Käthe Wulff under the name Schule für Eurythmie, and is soon forced to rename it again, since the word eurythmy has by now been claimed by Rudolf Steiner's anthroposophical movement for an entirely different discipline. The confusion of names tells its own story: an idea born of Dalcroze, refined by Laban, and now sovereign under Perrottet, must keep re-declaring what it is not in order to be recognized for what it is. It will eventually settle as simply the Bewegungsschule Suzanne Perrottet.

stops.name: Zurich, the lecture on the neglected body
stops.campa: She lectures publicly under the title Der vernachlässigte Körper und seine Forderungen, the neglected body and its demands, carrying the mountain's doctrine down into the language of civic reform: posture, breath and unhurried movement as public health, not merely artistic mysticism. Physicians in the audience take note; within a decade doctors like Max Bircher-Benner and even Carl Gustav Jung will be referring patients directly to her studio. Perrottet has found the form her whole career will take: dance as medicine for a century that broke its own body in the trenches.

stops.name: Zurich, Gluck's Iphigénie en Aulide, danced whole
stops.campa: She choreographs Christoph Willibald Gluck's Iphigénie en Aulide for the Zurich stage, turning her mountain vocabulary, tension, release, weight given and taken back, toward the eighteenth-century opera repertoire that Dalcroze himself once used to teach counted phrasing. The commission is a quiet act of reconciliation and conquest at once: the master she left is honored in the very medium she abandoned him for, danced now to music instead of against its absence, since even the sovereign body, she has learned, need not always dance in silence.

stops.name: Zurich, the Perrottet-Schoop years
stops.campa: For two years the school runs jointly with the young dancer Trudi Schoop, briefly renamed Bewegungsschule Perrottet-Schoop, a partnership between the mountain's first generation and its next. Schoop will go on to a career in grotesque and comic dance far from Laban's high seriousness, but she takes from Perrottet's studio the same root discipline every pupil here receives: the body trusted to invent its own necessity. Among the other names Perrottet trains in these years are Max Terpis and Vera Skoronel, both bound for their own places in the same expanding atlas of German dance.

stops.name: Zurich, the Zett-Haus, the school's futurist home
stops.campa: The school moves into the newly built Zett-Haus at Badenerstrasse 18, a startling glass-and-steel modernist block by the architects Flora Steiger-Crawford and Rudolf Steiger, a building as programmatically new as the movement taught inside it. Perrottet's studio takes its place among the building's other progressive tenants, the reformed body now housed in reformed architecture just as it was at Hellerau twenty years before, only this time the architecture and the choreography answer to no master but her.

stops.name: Lausanne, teaching the engineers to move
stops.campa: She is engaged to teach rhythmic gymnastics, body language and musical accompaniment at the École Polytechnique in Lausanne: precision-trained engineers sent to a dance pedagogue descended from Dalcroze and Laban both, to learn what their slide rules cannot give them. It is a strange late loop of her own itinerary: the canton where she was born, teaching the same discipline of counted and then uncounted movement to a generation that will build Switzerland's postwar infrastructure with hands she has, in some measure, first taught to be present in space.

stops.name: Zurich, the Landesausstellung of 1939
stops.campa: At the legendary Swiss National Exhibition on the Zürichhorn, the Landi, the great patriotic pageant mounted as Europe rearms around a determinedly neutral Switzerland, Perrottet's pupils perform, her movement pedagogy folded for one bright summer into the nation's own self-portrait. Forty years after the folk fair scenes of her own childhood on Lake Geneva, she stands inside a much larger and more anxious festival, teaching bodies to move well in a country trying to convince itself, and everyone else, that it will not be swallowed by the war massing at its borders.

stops.name: Zurich, the Swiss Professional Association founded
stops.campa: The same year, she co-founds the Schweizerischer Berufsverband für Tanz und Gymnastik, the Swiss professional association for dance and gymnastics, and sits on its committee for the next sixteen years. The itinerant art she once demonstrated on borrowed stages from Solothurn to Moscow now has a licensing body, a professional standard, a seat at the table of Swiss cultural bureaucracy. The revolutionary of Monte Verità has become, without renouncing anything, an institution: the surest sign a heresy has actually won.
